md_name: Soil microbial genomics under farm practices
md_description: This workflow represents the collection of soil samples from agricultural plots under different farming practices, followed by microbial DNA extraction, sequencing, and computational analysis. It produces raw sequencing data and derived microbial feature tables used to compare diversity and functional patterns across organic, conventional tillage, and no-till systems while associating observed environmental conditions such as pH, moisture, temperature, and crop type.

soil_sample_organic_plot.reasoning: For the organic plot soil sample entity, I included only intrinsic sample identity/origin and the field conditions explicitly associated with the collected soil specimen: plot management category, crop type, and in situ environmental measurements (pH, moisture, temperature) at collection. I excluded collection protocol details, extraction/sequencing settings, raw-read/file properties, and downstream computational outputs because those belong to Process, Capture, Signal, or Derivative nodes respectively. I also avoided sample/experiment identifiers if they might be repeated elsewhere, but since this node is the root sample entity in its branch, the schema focuses on the sample’s own descriptors without duplicating downstream fields.

md_schema.descr: Agricultural management practice of the source plot for this soil sample, recorded at sampling time. Use to indicate the farming system under which the sample was collected; typical values in this workflow are organic, conventional_tillage, and no_till.

Primary crop grown in the sampled plot at the time of soil collection, recorded as the field’s dominant crop or crop rotation stage. Example values: maize, soybean, wheat, cotton. Use a consistent crop name vocabulary.

In situ soil pH measured from the collected plot sample or adjacent field measurement at the time of sampling. Typical range 4.0–9.0 for agricultural soils; report on the pH scale used by the study, usually unitless.

Soil moisture content of the sampled plot at collection time, expressed as percent water content or gravimetric moisture percentage, depending on the field method used. Typical range 0–100 percent; record the sampling-point value nearest the collected core.

Soil temperature at the sampling point and time of collection, measured in degrees Celsius in the field near the collected sample. Typical agricultural range about -5 to 45 Celsius; record the temperature at or just before sample retrieval.
Material identity for this entity, indicating that the object is a soil sample collected from the field. Use this as a human-readable descriptor when multiple sample types may appear in the dataset.

Short free-text context describing the source plot and collection context for this soil sample, such as 'organic farm plot soil core' or similar. Use only for entity-level provenance; do not include extraction, sequencing, or analysis details here.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for this no-till plot soil sample, assigned at collection or intake. Use a stable string identifier such as 'NT-001' or a lab accession code; this field should identify the specific soil sample instance without repeating plot-management metadata.

Human-readable label for the field plot where the sample was collected, used to distinguish this no-till plot from other sampling locations in the study. Example values may include a farm plot code or block name such as 'Field A3' or 'North block'.

Brief free-text note describing the long-term management history of the source plot, specifically indicating no-till practice and any relevant prior field management context known at sampling. Use only a concise provenance note, not a protocol description.

Depth below the soil surface from which this sample was collected, measured in centimeters at the time of sampling. Typical agricultural soil core depths are 0–30 cm or 0–15 cm depending on study design; record the actual depth interval or depth point as a standardized string if needed.

Date and time when this no-till soil sample was collected in the field, recorded in ISO-like timestamp form when available (for example, 2026-08-18T09:30:00). Use this to support provenance and temporal ordering of samples.

md_schema.descr: Wet-lab DNA extraction approach used to isolate microbial DNA from the organic plot soil sample, recorded at the extraction step. Example methods include bead-beating plus silica column purification or phenol-chloroform extraction; use a consistent controlled term if available.

Commercial kit or protocol name used for DNA extraction, recorded for the organic sample extraction workflow. Example: DNeasy PowerSoil Kit. Use the exact kit name or protocol label as applied at the time of extraction.
Replicate index for this extraction if multiple extractions were performed on the same organic plot sample. Use an integer starting at 1 for the first extraction replicate.
Duration of any key lysis or incubation step during DNA extraction, measured in minutes at the time the organic soil sample was processed. Typical range 5–180 minutes depending on protocol.

Amount of purified DNA recovered from the organic plot soil sample after extraction, measured in nanograms at the end of the process. Typical environmental DNA yields can range from sub-ng to several micrograms depending on biomass and method.
Spectrophotometric purity ratio A260/A280 for the extracted DNA, measured on the purified DNA after extraction. Typical acceptable range is approximately 1.6–2.0 for DNA preparations.
Overall quality outcome of the extraction step for the organic plot sample, indicating whether the DNA extraction met the study’s minimum acceptance criteria for downstream sequencing.

md_schema.descr: Storage location or relative path of the raw sequencing reads file(s) generated from the organic plot DNA library. Use a stable URI, directory path, or object-store key, for example 's3://bucket/path/sample.fastq.gz'.

Number of read sequences contained in the organic raw reads artifact, counted from the raw file prior to trimming or filtering. This is a raw-data volume metric, typically from thousands to billions of reads.

Observed read length in base pairs for the organic raw reads artifact, as stored in the file. Use the dominant or nominal length when all reads are the same length; typical values are 50, 100, 150, or 250 bp depending on platform.
Indicator of whether the organic raw reads artifact contains paired-end sequencing data. Set true when forward and reverse reads are present, false when only single-end reads are present.

Approximate GC content percentage of the organic raw reads file, computed directly from the unprocessed reads as a technical composition metric. Typical metagenomic read GC percentages vary with community composition and library preparation.

Percentage of bases in the organic raw reads artifact with Phred quality score of 30 or higher, measured on the untrimmed sequencing output. Use this as a basic technical quality indicator for the raw data.

MD5 or equivalent checksum for the organic raw reads artifact, used to verify file integrity during storage and transfer. Record the checksum string exactly as produced by the archiving or transfer system.

Maximum number or fraction of ambiguous bases allowed in a read after QC for the conventional plot reads. Record the exact rule used by the trimming pipeline, such as an N-count cutoff.
Whether a host-removal or contaminant-filtering step was applied during QC of the conventional raw reads. Set true if reads matching a contaminant reference were removed; otherwise false.

Percentage of raw reads retained after QC trimming for the conventional plot sample, calculated as retained reads divided by input reads times 100. This is a process outcome/quality indicator measured at the end of QC.
Mean base quality score of the cleaned conventional reads after QC, used as a post-trimming quality indicator. Typical retained-read mean Q scores vary by platform and library quality.

read_qc_notill.reasoning: For the no-till read-QC process node, I included only process-level descriptors of how the raw reads were cleaned: software name/version, adapter strategy, quality threshold, minimum retained length, ambiguous-base handling, optional host removal, and output quality/retention indicators. md_schema.descr: Software used to trim and quality-filter the no-till plot raw reads, recorded as the process tool name. Example: fastp or similar read-cleaning software.
Version of the software used for trimming and quality filtering the no-till plot raw reads. Record the exact release string used in the pipeline, for example '0.23.4'.
Adapter removal strategy applied to the no-till raw reads during QC. Use a concise description such as automatic adapter detection, known adapter list, or platform-specific adapter set.
Minimum Phred quality threshold used to trim or filter low-quality bases from the no-till raw reads. Typical values are 20 or 30; record the threshold applied during QC.

Minimum read length in base pairs retained after trimming for the no-till plot reads. Reads shorter than this threshold are discarded; typical values range from 30 to 100 bp depending on pipeline design.
Maximum number or fraction of ambiguous bases allowed in a read after QC for the no-till plot reads. Record the exact rule used by the trimming pipeline, such as an N-count cutoff.
Whether a host-removal or contaminant-filtering step was applied during QC of the no-till raw reads. Set true if reads matching a contaminant reference were removed; otherwise false.

Percentage of raw reads retained after QC trimming for the no-till plot sample, calculated as retained reads divided by input reads times 100. This is a process outcome/quality indicator measured at the end of QC.
Mean base quality score of the cleaned no-till reads after QC, used as a post-trimming quality indicator. Typical retained-read mean Q scores vary by platform and library quality.

clean_reads_org.reasoning: For the organic clean-reads signal node, I included only raw/technical artifact metadata describing the cleaned read file itself: storage location, file format, size, sequence count, read length, paired-end status, GC content, Q30 percentage, and checksum. md_schema.descr: Storage location or relative path of the quality-filtered sequencing reads file(s) generated from the organic plot sample. Use a stable URI, directory path, or object-store key, for example 's3://bucket/path/sample.clean.fastq.gz'.

File format of the organic cleaned reads artifact, recorded as the raw sequence container format used by the pipeline after trimming and filtering. Common values include fastq, fastq_gz, bam, or ubam depending on storage conventions.

Total size of the organic cleaned reads file or file bundle in bytes, measured after QC and archiving. Use this to support storage and transfer auditing; typical sizes range from millions to billions of bytes depending on sequencing depth.
Number of read sequences contained in the organic cleaned reads artifact, counted after QC trimming and filtering. This is a post-QC data volume metric, typically from thousands to billions of reads.

Observed read length in base pairs for the organic cleaned reads artifact, as stored after QC. Use the dominant or nominal length when all reads are the same length; typical values are 50, 100, 150, or 250 bp depending on platform and trimming.
Indicator of whether the organic cleaned reads artifact contains paired-end sequencing data. Set true when forward and reverse reads are present, false when only single-end reads are present.

Approximate GC content percentage of the organic cleaned reads file, computed directly from the QC-filtered reads as a technical composition metric. Typical metagenomic read GC percentages vary with community composition and library preparation.

Percentage of bases in the organic cleaned reads artifact with Phred quality score of 30 or higher, measured on the QC-filtered output. Use this as a basic technical quality indicator for the cleaned data.

MD5 or equivalent checksum for the organic cleaned reads artifact, used to verify file integrity during storage and transfer. Record the checksum string exactly as produced by the archiving or transfer system.

joint_assembly.reasoning: For the joint assembly process node, I included only assembly-process metadata: assembler name/version, strategy for combining plots, key k-mer and contig length settings, minimum overlap or coverage thresholds, resource/runtime indicators, and assembly quality summaries such as N50 and total contig length. md_schema.descr: Assembler used to generate contigs from the combined clean reads across farm plots. Record the tool name used for metagenome assembly, such as MEGAHIT or an equivalent assembler.
Version of the assembly software used for the joint assembly step. Record the exact release string used in the workflow, for example '1.2.9'.

Description of how reads from the different farm plots were assembled, for example joint assembly across all clean reads or comparably assembled per plot with a common workflow. Use a concise categorical description of the assembly design.

List of k-mer sizes used by the assembler for the joint metagenome assembly, recorded in the run configuration. Typical values are a comma-separated series such as 21,33,55,77,99,127 depending on tool and read length.
Minimum contig length in base pairs retained from the assembly output. Contigs shorter than this threshold are discarded or not reported; common values are 500, 1000, or 2000 bp.

Minimum coverage or abundance threshold required for contig retention during assembly filtering, if applied. Report the value used by the workflow; typical values depend on assembler and dataset complexity.
Total runtime of the joint assembly process in minutes, measured from start of assembly to final contig generation. Use this as a computational process indicator.
Peak memory usage of the joint assembly process in gigabytes, recorded during execution on the compute system. Use this as a computational resource indicator.
Total length of all assembled contigs produced by the joint assembly process, in base pairs. This is a process-level quality/outcome indicator measured after assembly completes.
N50 statistic for the assembled contigs generated by the joint assembly process, reported in base pairs. This is a standard assembly quality indicator calculated after assembly completion.
Number of contigs produced by the joint assembly process after applying the minimum contig length filter. Record the final contig count as a summary of assembly output complexity.

assembled_contigs.reasoning: For the assembled contigs signal node, I included only artifact-level metadata describing the contig file itself: storage location, file format, size, contig count, total bases, length distribution, checksum, and basic technical content metrics. I excluded assembly parameters and runtime because those belong to the upstream assembly Process node, and I excluded downstream binning or annotation outputs because those belong to later Process/Derivative nodes. I used contig-specific names that do not overlap with the cleaned-read or assembly-process fields already generated.

md_schema.descr: Storage location or relative path of the assembled contig file generated from the joint assembly step. Use a stable URI, directory path, or object-store key, for example 's3://bucket/path/contigs.fasta'.

File format of the assembled contigs artifact, recorded as the sequence container format used by the assembly output. Common values include fasta, fa, or gzipped fasta depending on storage conventions.

Total size of the assembled contig file in bytes, measured after assembly and archiving. Use this to support storage and transfer auditing; file size typically depends on the number and length of contigs.
Number of contig sequences contained in the assembled contig file, counted after assembly output is written. This is a raw artifact volume metric, typically from hundreds to millions of contigs.
Sum of the lengths of all contigs contained in the assembly output, in base pairs. This is a technical content metric for the contig artifact and should be measured from the fasta file content.

N50 statistic computed directly from the contig file, reported in base pairs. Although commonly used as an assembly quality metric, here it describes the contig artifact itself as stored in the output file.
Approximate GC content percentage of the assembled contigs file, computed from the assembled sequences. This is a technical composition metric for the contig artifact.

MD5 or equivalent checksum for the assembled contig artifact, used to verify file integrity during storage and transfer. Record the checksum string exactly as produced by the archiving or transfer system.

binning.reasoning: For the binning process node, I included only process-level metadata describing how contigs were grouped into genome bins: binning software and version, algorithm settings, contig and coverage thresholds, marker/reference strategy, number of bins generated, and quality outcomes such as completeness and contamination summaries. I excluded contig file properties because those belong to the upstream Signal node, and I excluded MAG file properties because those belong to the downstream Derivative node. I also avoided fields that would duplicate the later MAG entity/derivative metadata by keeping the schema centered on the binning operation itself.

md_schema.descr: Software used to group assembled contigs into metagenome-assembled genome bins. Record the tool name used for binning, such as MetaBAT2 or an equivalent binning program.
Version of the binning software used for the metagenome binning step. Record the exact release string used in the workflow, for example '2.15'.

Algorithmic mode or binning strategy used by the software, for example single-sample binning, differential coverage binning, or hybrid binning. Use a concise categorical label for the configured binning mode.
Minimum contig length in base pairs required for a contig to be considered by the binning algorithm. Typical thresholds are 1000, 1500, or 2000 bp depending on dataset complexity.
Minimum contig coverage or abundance threshold used during binning, if applied. Report the value used by the workflow; typical thresholds depend on assembler and binning software.
Marker gene or reference marker set used to assess or guide binning quality, if applicable. Record the set name or profile database used for the binning run.
Number of genome bins produced by the binning process after filtering and refinement. This is a direct process output count measured at the end of binning.

Mean estimated completeness percentage of the produced genome bins, measured as a process quality outcome after binning. Typical values range from 0 to 100 percent depending on dataset quality and binning stringency.

Mean estimated contamination percentage of the produced genome bins, measured as a process quality outcome after binning. Typical values range from 0 to 100 percent, with lower values indicating cleaner bins.
Total runtime of the binning process in minutes, measured from the start of binning to final bin output. Use this as a computational process indicator.

mag_bins.reasoning: For the MAG bins derivative node, I included only computed-result metadata: bin identifiers, bin count, completeness and contamination, N50, genome size, GC content, coverage, taxonomy assignment, and basic naming/quality categories. I excluded binning algorithm settings and runtime because those belong to the upstream binning Process node, and I excluded contig artifact properties because those belong to the upstream contig Signal node. I also avoided using names already generated for the organic/conventional/no-till branches by focusing on MAG-level computed outputs rather than upstream inputs.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the metagenome-assembled genome bin. Use a stable string accession or bin label such as 'bin.001' or a study-specific MAG ID; this identifies the derived genome bin itself.

Number of genome bins represented in this derived MAG collection or table if the node stores a multi-bin result set. If the node stores one row per bin, use this as a summary count for the full derivative object.

Estimated completeness percentage of the MAG, calculated from marker gene recovery or equivalent genome completeness estimation. Typical values range from 0 to 100 percent; measured after binning and refinement.
Estimated contamination percentage of the MAG, calculated from marker gene redundancy or equivalent purity assessment. Typical values range from 0 to 100 percent; lower values indicate cleaner bins.
N50 statistic for the MAG sequence set, reported in base pairs. This is a computed assembly/binned-genome quality indicator measured from the finalized MAG contig set.
Estimated total genome size of the MAG in base pairs, calculated from the final binned contigs or completeness-corrected estimate. Typical bacterial MAG sizes are on the order of 0.5 to 10 Mbp.
GC content percentage of the MAG, computed from the binned contigs. This is a derived composition metric used for genome characterization.

Mean sequencing coverage of the MAG across the contributing cleaned reads, used as an abundance or support metric for the derived genome. Report the coverage value from the binning/coverage estimation workflow.

Taxonomic label assigned to the MAG by downstream classification methods. Example values may include phylum, genus, or species-level labels depending on confidence, such as 'Proteobacteria' or 'Bacillus sp.'.
Quality category assigned to the MAG based on completeness and contamination thresholds. Use a controlled label such as high_quality, medium_quality, or low_quality if the study applies such bins.

annotation.reasoning: For the annotation process node, I included only process-level fields describing how MAGs were annotated: annotation software, version, database/source, gene-calling settings, functional ontology mappings, and process outcome counts/quality indicators. I excluded MAG intrinsic properties because those belong to the upstream Derivative node, and I excluded downstream function-table file properties because those belong to the function_table Derivative node. I kept the schema focused on the annotation operation itself so it remains reproducible without duplicating output-table metadata.

md_schema.descr: Software used to annotate the recovered genome bins and infer genes or functional potential. Record the tool name used for annotation, such as Prokka or an equivalent genome annotation program.
Version of the annotation software used for the MAG annotation step. Record the exact release string used in the workflow, for example '1.14.6'.
Reference database or resource used during MAG annotation, such as a protein family database, gene catalog, or taxonomic reference set. Record the database name and version if available.
Gene-calling or ORF prediction mode used during annotation, if configurable. Use a concise label for the configured mode or prediction strategy applied to the genome bins.
Functional ontology or classification system used to assign annotations, such as GO, KEGG, COG, or a study-specific ontology. Use a controlled label for the main annotation scheme.

Minimum coding sequence or protein-coding region length, in base pairs, used as a filter during annotation or gene prediction. Typical values depend on the annotation pipeline and gene-calling settings.
Total number of genes or open reading frames predicted across the annotated MAG set. This is a process outcome measured after annotation completes.
Number of predicted genes that received at least one functional assignment from the annotation workflow. This is a process-level quality/output indicator.
Total runtime of the annotation process in minutes, measured from the start of gene prediction to final functional annotation output. Use this as a computational process indicator.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the derived functional profile table. Use a stable string accession or table label such as 'func_table_001' or a study-specific result ID.

Number of rows in the derived functional table, counted after the table is written. Use this as a table dimension metric for the number of gene or feature entries represented.
Number of columns in the derived functional table, counted after the table is written. Use this as a table dimension metric for the number of samples, genomes, or functional categories represented.
Total number of genes included in the functional table with at least one annotation or feature assignment. This is a computed summary of the derived output.
Number of distinct functional labels or categories represented in the derived functional table, such as unique genes, pathways, or ontology terms. Measure after table construction.
Fraction of table entries with nonzero or non-null values, used as a sparsity indicator for the derived functional matrix. Typical values depend on table design and normalization strategy.

MD5 or equivalent checksum for the derived functional table artifact, used to verify file integrity during storage and transfer. Record the checksum string exactly as produced by the archiving or transfer system.

Short free-text summary of the derived functional table contents, such as the dominant functional categories represented or a brief note on normalization. Keep this focused on the final computed table rather than the annotation pipeline.

diversity_analysis.reasoning: For the diversity analysis process node, I included only computational-analysis metadata: the statistical framework, software and version, comparison design across farming practices, diversity metrics, functional metrics, covariates, significance thresholds, correction method, and summary outcome indicators. I excluded upstream MAG/function-table properties because those belong to the input Derivative nodes, and I excluded downstream result file properties because those belong to the comparative_results Derivative node. md_schema.descr: Software or analysis environment used for the diversity comparison step, such as R or an ecological statistics package. Record the tool name used to perform the comparative analysis.
Version of the statistical or analysis software used for the diversity analysis step. Record the exact release string, for example '4.4'.

Design of the comparison performed across farming practices, indicating how organic, conventional tillage, and no-till samples or derived genomes were contrasted. Use a concise study-design label such as pairwise, all_groups, or mixed_model.
Primary alpha or beta diversity metric used in the comparison, such as Shannon, Simpson, Bray-Curtis, or UniFrac. Record the main metric applied in this analysis step.

Primary functional comparison metric used for gene or pathway profiles, such as richness, abundance, pathway coverage, or differential abundance. Record the main functional measure used in the analysis.

List or description of environmental covariates included in the diversity analysis model, such as soil pH, moisture, temperature, or crop type. Record the variables adjusted for in the statistical comparison.

Multiple-testing correction method applied in the diversity analysis, if any. Use a controlled label such as FDR, Bonferroni, or none.
Number of taxa, bins, genes, or functional features tested in the comparative analysis. This is a computational analysis summary measured from the input data at the end of the analysis step.
Number of features found significant under the chosen threshold and correction method. This is a key outcome indicator for the diversity analysis process.
Summary of effect sizes estimated in the comparison, such as fold-change, log2 fold-change, or standardized effect sizes. Record the main effect-size summary used by the analysis workflow.

comparative_results.reasoning: For the comparative results derivative node, I included only computed result metadata describing the final analysis artifact and its summarized findings: result table/file location and format, dimensions, number of comparisons, p-value and effect-size summaries, significant outcome counts, visualization/summary artifact links, and checksum. I excluded analysis settings and statistical method details because those belong to the upstream diversity_analysis Process node, and I excluded upstream MAG/function-table properties because those are inputs to the analysis rather than properties of the final result object. md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the derived comparative results object. Use a stable string accession or result label such as 'comp_results_001' or a study-specific analysis ID.
Storage location or relative path of the final comparative results file. Use a stable URI, directory path, or object-store key, for example 's3://bucket/path/comparative_results.tsv'.
File format of the final comparative results artifact. Common values include tsv, csv, parquet, html, or pdf depending on how the results are stored and shared.
Number of rows in the final comparative results table or matrix, counted after the result file is written. Use this as a dimension metric for the reported comparisons or features.
Number of columns in the final comparative results table or matrix, counted after the result file is written. Use this as a dimension metric for the reported summary statistics or sample groups.
Number of pairwise or groupwise comparisons included in the final result set. Measure this after analysis completes, based on the reported contrast structure.
Number of comparative findings meeting the analysis significance threshold in the final results object. This is a key summary outcome of the differential or ecological comparison step.
Summary of p-values reported in the final comparative results, such as minimum, median, or adjusted p-value summary. Use a concise textual or numeric summary of the result set’s statistical support.

Summary of effect sizes reported in the final comparative results, such as fold-change ranges, log2 fold-change medians, or standardized effect size summaries. Record the main effect-size characterization of the result set.
Storage location or URI of a figure, report, or visualization that summarizes the final comparative results. Example: a PDF, HTML report, or image file generated from the analysis.

MD5 or equivalent checksum for the final comparative results artifact, used to verify file integrity during storage and transfer. Record the checksum string exactly as produced by the archiving or transfer system.
